overview: Tower Limited is a New Zealand-headquartered general insurer providing home, contents, motor, boat and some commercial/rural insurance to retail and SME customers, with a core New Zealand business plus operations across several Pacific Island nations (Fiji, Papua New Guinea, and other Pacific markets). Tower is the largest NZX-listed general insurer, positioned as a direct (largely broker-light) personal lines and SME specialist competing against much larger bank-owned and Australian-parented insurers. Fiscal year ends 30 September; the company reports under IFRS 17 (Insurance revenue basis) since FY2024.

business_model.summary: Tower underwrites general insurance policies and earns premium income (Gross Written Premium) net of reinsurance costs and claims expense, supplemented by investment income on its policyholder and shareholder funds. Revenue is largely recurring/renewal-based (annual policy renewals) rather than project-based, with growth driven by customer/policy count, pricing (risk-based pricing model), and cross-sell of partnership-distributed products. A significant reinsurance program cedes large-event/catastrophe risk to global reinsurers, smoothing earnings volatility from natural catastrophes (a defining structural feature of NZ general insurance given earthquake, flood and cyclone exposure).

revenue_streams.name: New Zealand home/house insurance
revenue_streams.trend: growing (11% policy growth FY25, 9% in H1 FY26)

revenue_streams.name: Partnership-distributed GWP (Kiwibank referral, Westpac NZ from Jul-2026)
Net investment income (float on policyholder/shareholder funds)
revenue_streams.trend: declining in FY26 amid lower NZ interest rates

business_model.customer_type: B2C retail personal lines (house, contents, motor) plus SME/commercial, direct-to-consumer distribution supplemented by bank/retail partnerships
business_model.geographic_mix: Predominantly New Zealand (core house insurance is the strategic growth focus), with a smaller Pacific Islands General Insurance segment; NZ$ reporting currency, dual-listed NZX/ASX

main_competitors: IAG NZ (AMI, State, NZI, Lumley, Lantern brands)
Ando, Delta Insurance and other niche/direct players
competitive_position.market_position: Tower is the largest NZX-listed standalone general insurer but a distant challenger to the two dominant groups: IAG (AMI/State/NZI) and Suncorp/AA Insurance, which together hold roughly 65-70% of the New Zealand personal lines market. Tower differentiates as a direct, digitally-enabled, data-driven underwriter rather than competing on branch/broker scale.

moat_factors.description: First NZ insurer to introduce address-level risk-based pricing for earthquake (2018) and flood (2021), now extended to landslide and sea surge (Aug 2025) using Moody's, Haskoning and Swiss Re models; supports more precise underwriting and reduced cross-subsidisation versus flat-rate competitors

59% of NZ customers registered for My Tower, 70% of claims lodged digitally, AI-enabled contact centre (built with Deloitte/AWS) launched Aug-2025; supports lower management expense ratio over time and improved NPS (+44 in FY25)
Referral/underwriting partnerships with Kiwibank and a new long-term Westpac NZ agreement (from Jul-2026) provide low-cost customer acquisition channels that smaller/direct-only rivals lack

Canstar Home & Contents Insurer of the Year (2 years running) is a positive, but reputation has been damaged by the multi-policy-discount conduct failure and $7m FMA penalty (Dec 2025), a headwind to trust-based brand equity
Tower is materially smaller than IAG NZ (~$4.1bn GWP) and Suncorp NZ (~$2.8bn GWP) group-wide, limiting reinsurance buying power and fixed-cost leverage relative to the two dominant players

weaknesses: Small scale relative to IAG and Suncorp/AA limits pricing power and reinsurance terms
High customer concentration risk to NZ natural catastrophe/weather events (no true geographic diversification outside NZ/Pacific)
History of conduct/regulatory failures (MPD mispricing) has damaged trust and consumed management bandwidth and capital
Declining average premiums (mix shift to lower-risk, lower-premium policies) constrains GWP growth even as policy count grows
MER (~31%) has been sticky/rising, reflecting continued technology investment amid a soft pricing cycle

growth_drivers: Continued NZ house insurance policy growth (core strategic focus; 11% growth FY25, 9% in H1 FY26) as Tower targets share gains in its highest-priority product line
New distribution partnerships — Westpac NZ underwriting agreement commencing July 2026 and expanded Kiwibank back-book referral arrangement, both starting H2 FY26
Expansion of risk-based pricing (landslide, sea surge added Aug-2025) enabling targeted pricing to win lower-risk business while re-pricing/managing higher-risk exposure

Digital/AI-enabled claims and contact-centre transformation (AI-enabled contact centre with Deloitte/AWS, straight-through-repair for motor and house) targeting structurally lower management expense ratio over time
Softer reinsurance cost trend — catastrophe reinsurance-to-GWP ratio has fallen from ~13.9% (FY24) to 13.3% (FY25) to an estimated 10.7% (FY26), a direct tailwind to underlying margins if it persists
Customer base growth (318,000 in FY25, up from 305,000; 327,000 by H1 FY26, +5% YoY) supporting a larger, more diversified policy book

business.description: As a NZ/Pacific-concentrated general insurer, Tower's earnings are structurally exposed to earthquakes, floods, cyclones and storms; FY26 has already seen four large events costing $18.5m in H1 plus an estimated $5m Wellington flood (Apr-2026) event, versus a much more benign FY25/H1 FY25

business.risk: Competitive/pricing pressure from IAG and Suncorp/AA
business.description: Average premiums have declined due to mix shift to lower-risk policies and heightened competition; GWP growth guidance for FY26 was cut to low-single-digits from 5-10% previously
MPD remediation programme (~$12m to affected customers) is nearing completion but reputational and process risk persists; management attention diverted from growth initiatives
Growing reliance on bank partnerships (Kiwibank, Westpac) for growth introduces counterparty/contract-renewal risk over the medium term

financial.risk: Investment income sensitivity to interest rates
financial.description: H1 FY26 net investment income fell to $5.1m from $10.0m in H1 FY25, explicitly attributed to lower yields amid NZ rate-cutting cycle; a further tailwind reversal if rates fall further

Although FY26 reinsurance costs fell to an estimated 10.7% of GWP, this is a global reinsurance market subject to hardening cycles after major catastrophe years; a hard market would compress margins or require higher retentions

NZ parent solvency margin was $89m (143% solvency ratio) at FY25 year-end — comfortable, but large-event years or the compulsory $45m capital return in FY25 illustrate capital can be drawn down quickly

regulatory.description: Tower paid a $7m FMA penalty (High Court ruling, 9-Dec-2025) plus ~$11.7m in customer remediation over the multi-policy-discount conduct failure (2016-2025, ~61,000-90,000 policies affected); ongoing CoFI (Conduct of Financial Institutions) licensing obligations raise compliance costs across the industry

NZ Government's planned Climate Adaptation Framework legislation could reshape managed retreat, insurability and risk-sharing arrangements for high-risk properties, with direct implications for Tower's underwriting appetite and pricing
Ongoing RBNZ solvency standard reviews and potential increases in capital requirements for general insurers

macro.description: Subdued NZ economic conditions are cited by management as contributing to affordability-driven mix shift toward lower-premium policies and softer GWP growth
Falling NZ interest rates reduce investment income on Tower's substantial investment portfolio (~$326m at Mar-2026), a direct drag on profit already evident in H1 FY26
Increasing frequency/severity of extreme weather events in NZ and the Pacific raises both claims costs and reinsurance costs structurally over time

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ general insurance market is mature and concentrated (IAG and Suncorp/AA control ~65-70%), with modest underlying premium growth offset by episodic catastrophe losses; industry-wide focus on risk-based pricing, climate adaptation and conduct regulation (CoFI) is reshaping competitive dynamics
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate-to-high — earnings are non-cyclical from a demand perspective (insurance is close to compulsory for mortgaged property) but highly volatile year-to-year due to weather/catastrophe events and the reinsurance cost cycle
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate — falling rates directly reduce investment income (evident in H1 FY26 decline), though liabilities are not debt-funded (Tower carries no borrowings, only IFRS-16 lease liabilities)
key_input_costs: Reinsurance premiums (global catastrophe reinsurance market pricing)
Claims costs (building materials, motor parts, repair labour inflation)

recent_developments.event: H1 FY2026 results: reported NPAT of $22.9m (down 54% YoY from $49.7m), underlying NPAT of $36.8m (down from $61.7m); interim dividend declared at 5c/share; FY26 GWP guidance cut to low-single-digit growth from 5-10%; underlying NPAT guidance reaffirmed at $55m-$65m for FY26
Wellington flooding/severe weather event generated fewer than 130 claims for Tower (industry-wide ~500+ across IAG brands); to be booked as an estimated $5m large event in H2 FY26

High Court ordered Tower to pay a $7m penalty to the FMA for misleading multi-policy-discount representations (2016-2025); Tower had already repaid ~$11.7m to affected customers and provisioned $10.3m for remediation/penalty as of FY25

Tower successfully renewed its FY26 reinsurance programme: catastrophe upper limit raised to $915m (from $800m), reinsurance cost estimated to fall to 10.7% of GWP (from 13.3% in FY25), reflecting a softer global reinsurance market and multi-year reinsurer relationships

FY25 results: record underlying profit of $107.2m (vs $83.5m FY24), reported profit $83.7m (vs $74.3m FY24); BAU claims ratio improved to 41% (from 48%) on benign weather; GWP grew 2% to $600m; full-year dividend 24.5c/share, including a special component from under-utilised large-event allowance

Expanded risk-based pricing to landslide and sea surge risk (in addition to existing earthquake/flood models), with >90% of existing customers to see reductions in the natural-hazards portion of their premium at renewal from Oct-2025
Launched AI-enabled contact centre platform (built with Deloitte and AWS/Amazon Connect)

Leadership transition: Paul Johnston (previously CFO since Jan-2022) appointed CEO (Jun-2025); Naomi Ballantyne joined the Board (May-2025) and later became Chair; new Chief Data & Analytics Officer and Chief Digital & Technology Officer appointments (Nov-2025)
New long-term underwriting/distribution partnership with Westpac NZ to supply general insurance products to Westpac's retail customers, commencing July 2026

items.notes: Reaffirmed from FY25 result guidance; assumes full utilisation of the $45m large-event allowance; well below FY25 underlying profit of $107.2m given a much more benign FY25 weather comparative
Down from prior 5%-10% guidance, due to lower average premiums (mix shift, competitive pricing) and subdued NZ market conditions
Reflects ongoing investment in growth, technology and customer experience initiatives against a soft premium cycle
$18.5m already utilised in H1 FY26 (4 large events) plus an estimated $5m Wellington flood event booked in H2; approximately $21.5m of the allowance remained available for H2 as of the H1 release

items.target: trending up through FY26 but remaining below long-run average (48-50%)
items.notes: H1 FY26 BAU claims ratio was 44%, up from an unusually low 38% in H1 FY25
Down from 13.3% in FY25, reflecting FY26 reinsurance renewal on more favourable terms

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Paul Johnston characterised H1 FY26 as reflecting Tower's positive long-term earnings trajectory but against an exceptionally strong prior-year comparative (unusually benign weather in H1 FY25). Management stated it does not expect the challenging operating environment (pricing pressure, elevated weather claims, global volatility) to improve in H2 FY26, and reiterated FY26 underlying NPAT guidance of $55m-$65m is achievable assuming full utilisation of the large-event allowance, with growth increasingly expected to come from digitisation/efficiency and new distribution partnerships (Westpac, Kiwibank) rather than premium increases.

bull_case: Strong balance sheet with no borrowings, comfortable solvency (143% ratio, $89m margin at FY25) and a track record of capital returns (special dividends, $45m compulsory buyback in FY25)

Softening reinsurance market is a structural tailwind — reinsurance cost/GWP has fallen from ~13.9% to an estimated 10.7% over two renewal cycles, directly supporting underlying margins if the trend persists

New, largely incremental distribution partnerships (Westpac NZ from Jul-2026, expanded Kiwibank referral) provide low-cost growth channels beyond organic pricing, alongside continued double-digit house-policy growth

Digital/AI investment (My Tower, AI-enabled contact centre, straight-through claims processing) is measurably improving efficiency (MER, NPS, digital task completion) and should support margin expansion once the platform matures

Risk-based pricing leadership (first mover on earthquake/flood, now landslide/sea surge) should improve long-term underwriting quality and reduce large-event volatility relative to flat-rate competitors
bear_case: H1 FY26 profit decline (-54% YoY) illustrates the structural earnings volatility of a small, geographically concentrated general insurer — a run of below-average weather years can quickly reverse a strong FY25

GWP growth guidance was cut in-year (5-10% to low-single-digit), showing competitive/pricing pressure from IAG and Suncorp/AA is intensifying and constraining topline growth despite policy count gains

Repeated conduct/regulatory failures (MPD mispricing, $7m FMA penalty, ~$12m customer remediation) signal execution and systems weaknesses that carry both financial and reputational cost, and CoFI compliance costs are structurally rising
Investment income is shrinking as NZ interest rates fall, removing a profit tailwind at the same time BAU claims and large-event costs are normalizing upward from FY25's unusually benign base

Small scale versus IAG (~$4.1bn GWP) and Suncorp/AA (~$2.8bn GWP) limits pricing power, reinsurance terms and cost leverage, making Tower a perpetual share-taker in a market dominated by two much larger, bank/insurance-group-backed rivals
